followUps: Because verify already runs every phase that install does except the last copy into ~/.m2, so install adds nothing for a CI job. A fresh CI workspace has no old target/, so clean is also unneeded. Installing snapshots into the shared local repo can even hide a missing-dependency bug on later builds. Use mvn -B verify.

Name the plugin and goal: mvn compiler:compile or mvn surefire:test; the full form is groupId:artifactId:version:goal. Running a goal runs only that goal, not earlier phases, so the files it needs (such as target/classes) must already exist. Running a phase instead runs every earlier phase. mvn help:describe -Dplugin=compiler lists a plugin's goals.

Same phases as jar packaging, but a different plugin is bound to package. The <packaging>war</packaging> element picks the binding: resources:resources, compiler:compile, surefire:test, then war:war instead of jar:jar, then install and deploy as usual. mvn help:effective-pom shows what is bound.

compileOnly. It puts the library on the compile classpath only, not on the runtime classpath or in consumers' dependencies. Gradle does not share it with tests, so add testImplementation (or testCompileOnly) too, whereas Maven's provided is visible to tests. The war plugin also offers providedCompile.

Because compile scope ships in the artifact and is passed on to everyone who depends on you. JUnit would end up inside your fat jar (a couple of MB extra), on production classpaths, and in your consumers' dependency trees where it can clash with their own test library versions. test scope keeps it out of all three.

code.title: Maven nearest-wins version resolution
code.python:
from collections import deque

# Dependency graph: artifact -> list of (child, version) in declaration order
graph = {
    "app": [("A", "1.0"), ("B", "1.0")],
    "A": [("C", "1.0")],
    "B": [("D", "1.0")],
    "D": [("C", "2.0")],
}

def resolve(root, direct):
    # Breadth-first walk: the shallowest path wins ("nearest wins"), ties go to first declared
    chosen = {}
    queue = deque(direct)
    while queue:
        name, ver = queue.popleft()
        if name in chosen:
            print("  omit %s:%s (conflict with %s)" % (name, ver, chosen[name]))
            continue
        chosen[name] = ver
        print("  pick %s:%s" % (name, ver))
        queue.extend(graph.get(name, []))  # children of a loser are never added
    print("  => C resolves to " + chosen["C"])

print("Scenario 1: transitive only")
resolve("app", graph["app"])
print("Scenario 2: app pins C:3.0 directly")
resolve("app", [("C", "3.0")] + graph["app"])

followUps: By default Gradle picks the highest version among the candidates, so C 1.0 versus C 2.0 gives 2.0, where Maven's nearest-wins gave 1.0. strictly pins an exact version and fails if something needs another one. failOnVersionConflict() makes the build fail on any conflict instead of resolving it silently.

Shade when two libraries need incompatible versions of the same dependency, or when you publish a library that must not leak its dependencies. maven-shade-plugin copies the classes into your jar and relocates packages, for example com.google.common to com.acme.shaded.common, rewriting bytecode references. The cost is a bigger jar and harder debugging.

They are dropped. Only the winning node contributes its own dependencies. If C 2.0 loses to C 1.0 and C 2.0 needed library E, then E is not on the classpath unless another path brings it, which shows up at runtime as NoClassDefFoundError. This is why you read dependency:tree -Dverbose after changing versions.

A parent is single inheritance and passes down everything: properties, dependencies, plugins and dependencyManagement. A BOM import passes only the version list, through <scope>import</scope><type>pom</type> inside dependencyManagement, and you can import several. Use a parent for shared build setup, and a BOM for versions when you already have a parent.

Set the version property the BOM reads, for example <jackson-bom.version>2.17.2</jackson-bom.version> in <properties> (Gradle: ext['jackson-bom.version'] = '2.17.2'). Or declare the artifact in your own dependencyManagement before the import, because the first declaration wins. Always re-run the tests, since you left the tested set.

A task is cacheable when its inputs and outputs are fully declared and it is deterministic: same inputs, same outputs, no hidden dependence on time, absolute paths or environment variables. Gradle hashes the inputs into a key; on a hit it restores the outputs and reports FROM-CACHE. Custom tasks opt in with @CacheableTask. compileJava with the same sources, classpath and JDK is the standard example.

First measure, then fix the biggest cost. Typical steps: stop using clean; build in parallel with -T 1C; build only affected modules with -pl X -am; run tests in parallel forks; use a build-cache extension or the mvnd daemon; move slow integration tests to a separate stage. A 12 minute build often drops to 4 or 5.

-rf :module-c (resume from) restarts the reactor at that module after you fixed a failure, skipping the modules before it. Example: mvn verify -rf :module-c. The skipped modules' outputs are not in the reactor any more, so they must already be in the local repo (use install earlier) or the build may not resolve them.

Maven sorts the reactor before building anything and fails at once with "The projects in the reactor contain a cyclic reference", so even mvn validate in CI catches it in seconds. Gradle also refuses a circular project dependency. For package-level cycles inside one module, add an ArchUnit rule so a new cycle fails a test.

When the repo is a very large monorepo, often multi-language, and you need hermetic builds, exact incremental correctness and remote execution across thousands of targets. The price is BUILD files everywhere, a steep learning curve and a migration. For a service with ten modules, Maven or Gradle with a remote cache is simpler.

code.title: JUnit 5 style lifecycle: new instance per test, AfterEach even on failure

followUps: Outer first going in, inner first going out. For one test the order is: outer @BeforeEach, inner @BeforeEach, the test, inner @AfterEach, outer @AfterEach. So the outer setup can build the shared object and the inner setup adds the scenario. Nested classes are non-static inner classes, so a @BeforeAll in one needs @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) on Java versions before 16.

Because the tests share state or depend on order. Typical causes: a static field or singleton cache that test A changes and test B reads, rows left in a database, the current time, or parallel execution. Example: A sets a static counter to 1 and B expects 0, so B passes alone but fails after A. Fix it by resetting in @BeforeEach and avoiding shared mutable statics. Random method order helps expose it.

code.title: Table-driven test: one body, many rows at the boundary

followUps:
Put the file on the test classpath and use @CsvFileSource; each of the 500 rows becomes its own invocation in the report.

@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0}")
@CsvFileSource(resources = "/cases.csv", numLinesToSkip = 1)
void rule(String name, int in, int expected) {
  assertEquals(expected, shipping(in));
}
If rows need objects, load the file in a @MethodSource. 500 pure in-memory rows run in well under a second.

Property-based testing states a rule that must hold for any input, and a framework such as jqwik generates hundreds of random inputs and shrinks a failure to the smallest one. It is better when the rule is general, for example reverse(reverse(x)) == x or "sorted output is ordered and has the same size". Example-based tests stay better for specific business values like "49.99 pays shipping".

code.title: Stub, fake, spy and mock written by hand

followUps: London (mockist) isolates each class with mocks, verifies the interactions, and designs outside-in. Chicago (classicist) uses real objects and fakes, verifies the result or state, and doubles only at the boundaries. London tests pinpoint failures but break more easily when you refactor; Chicago tests survive refactoring but one bug can fail several tests.

Because a mock only encodes your guess about how the third-party library behaves, so it keeps passing after the library changes, and you cannot shape its API to be easy to mock. Wrap it in your own small interface, mock that wrapper in unit tests, and test the wrapper against the real library once in an integration test. Example: wrap HttpClient in RateClient.fetch().

Mockito's strict stubs (the default with MockitoExtension) fail the test when a stub was set up but never used. It means dead setup or that the code no longer takes that path, for example you stubbed charge("u1", 500) but the service now charges 600. Remove the stub, fix the arguments, or mark shared setup lenient() if it is deliberately unused in some tests.

Use try (MockedStatic<Clock> m = mockStatic(Clock.class)) { m.when(Clock::now).thenReturn(t); ... }; it works only on the current thread and must be closed (inline mock maker, default since Mockito 5). Avoid it in new code: a static call is a hidden dependency, so inject a Clock or a small wrapper instead. Keep static mocking for legacy code you cannot change yet.

Mockito checks stubbings from the latest to the earliest and the last matching one wins. If you write when(f("x")).thenReturn(B) and later when(f(any())).thenReturn(A), then f("x") returns A, because the broad matcher is newer. Always stub the general case first and the specific cases after it.

mock(Foo.class, CALLS_REAL_METHODS) creates a mock with no real state: the constructor does not run and fields are default (null or 0), but unstubbed methods run real code, so they may throw NullPointerException. spy(obj) instead copies the state of a real, fully built instance. Use the partial mock for abstract classes or default interface methods, and the spy when an object already exists.

Extract the expensive or awkward part behind an interface and inject it. Example: PriceService has fetchRate() (an HTTP call) and compute(). Move fetchRate() to a RateClient interface passed to the constructor. The test then gives it a stub or fake and runs the real compute(), with no spy and no real HTTP.

Mount the host's Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) into the CI job, or run the job on a VM runner that has its own Docker daemon, or point DOCKER_HOST at a remote daemon (or use Testcontainers Cloud). The socket mount avoids a nested daemon, but gives the job root-level power over the host, so use it only on trusted, ephemeral runners.

Clean the data, not the container. Truncate tables in @BeforeEach (TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE takes milliseconds, restarting a container several seconds), or give each test unique ids. @Transactional rollback works for @DataJpaTest, but does not cover data committed from other threads. Schema-per-class is another option when tests run in parallel.

Because a hard-coded <argLine> in the Surefire config replaces the -javaagent option that jacoco:prepare-agent had stored in the argLine property, so the agent never starts, no jacoco.exec is written, and the report shows 0%. Fix: use late replacement, <argLine>@{argLine} -Xmx1g</argLine>.

Each module writes its own jacoco.exec. In Maven add a report module that depends on all of them and runs jacoco:report-aggregate; in Gradle use the jacoco-report-aggregation plugin. Gate on the aggregate when module tests cover each other's code, and per module for libraries. A per-module report undercounts classes that other modules' tests exercise.

Start many threads with the same idempotency key, release them together, and assert exactly one charge:

var go = new CountDownLatch(1);
var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20);
futures = 20 x pool.submit(() -> { go.await(); return svc.pay(key, 500); });
go.countDown();
assertEquals(1, gatewayCharges.get());
Also assert all 20 responses carry the same receipt id. Run it on a real PostgreSQL so the unique constraint on the key is exercised.

The consumer writes the expectations (for example a Pact file) and publishes them to a broker. The provider verifies them in its own CI on every build, and the consumer verifies against generated stubs. The consumer owns what it needs; the provider owns keeping the contract green. A can-i-deploy check gates each release so a breaking change fails before it ships.

Do not just rerun it. Reproduce by running it 50 times in a loop, then find the cause: a sleep where it should wait, shared data, test order, or the clock. Quarantine it with a tag and a ticket that has an owner and a deadline so it stops blocking the pipeline. Then fix the root cause, for example replace sleep with Awaitility, or isolate its data. Delete it if it has no value.
